\begin{abstract}
This paper investigates grant-free random access in low Earth orbit
satellite Internet-of-Things systems without global navigation satellite
system (GNSS) assistance. To handle large differential delays and
Doppler shifts across devices, we propose a multi-frame affine
frequency division multiplexing (AFDM) transmission scheme and analyze
its input-output relationship. Based on this model, we learn a
score-based generative prior directly from AFDM effective-channel
samples, without imposing sparse or grid-aligned channel assumptions.
The finite-dimensional, structured multi-frame AFDM observation model
may cause a mismatch between denoiser-input errors and white Gaussian
noise used for training. We therefore train the channel
denoiser using colored Gaussian noise with different covariance matrices.
The learned prior is then incorporated into a message-passing (MP)
receiver with two modules: multi-frame linear estimation (MFLE), which
suppresses inter-user interference; and generative-prior-aided joint
denoising (GPJD), which performs minimum mean-squared error (MMSE)
denoising.
To reduce errors associated with a Gaussian approximation of the channel
posterior, GPJD employs a learned density-ratio estimator to obtain
posterior probabilities of activity.
The two modules iteratively exchange soft information for joint activity
detection and channel estimation (JADCE). Numerical simulations demonstrate
that the proposed receiver
outperforms the baseline receiver in activity detection and channel
estimation.
\end{abstract}
% GP-MP-CCD algorithm revision; current result figures are included in Section VI.
\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Affine frequency division multiplexing, grant-free
random access, joint activity detection and channel estimation,
score-based generative models.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Sixth-generation (6G) wireless networks are expected to provide ubiquitous
connectivity for a massive number of Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices
\cite{cai2026,xu2026}. To serve devices in remote areas with limited terrestrial
coverage, low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites complement cellular networks for
applications such as smart agriculture and climate monitoring \cite{shen2025,kodheli2021}. These
power-limited devices transmit short packets sporadically, with only a small
fraction active at a given time \cite{shen2025,cai2026,mei2022}. In grant-based random
access, handshaking before transmission incurs significant
signaling overhead, while the long propagation delay of terrestrial-satellite links
further increases access latency \cite{cai2026,xu2026}. Accordingly, grant-free
random access (GFRA) allows active devices to transmit pilots and data directly
without first obtaining a grant, reducing signaling overhead and access latency in LEO satellite IoT
systems \cite{cai2026,xu2026}.

Supporting GFRA over LEO links requires handling large delays and Doppler shifts
caused by long propagation distances and high satellite mobility. The 3rd Generation
Partnership Project (3GPP) Release 17 framework addresses these effects through
device-side precompensation assisted by the global navigation satellite system
(GNSS) \cite{3gpp38300}. With such precompensation, many existing satellite GFRA
schemes assume perfect compensation or small residual delays and Doppler shifts at
the receiver \cite{shen2025}. Frequent estimation and compensation increase
energy consumption and reduce battery lifetime, making these schemes less suitable
for power-limited remote IoT devices \cite{shen2025}. This motivates reducing
dependence on GNSS, consistent with the GNSS-independent operation considered in the
Release 19 study on satellite access \cite{3gpp22865}. With reduced reliance on
device-side precompensation, the satellite receiver must accommodate
large differential delays and Doppler shifts, which can cause severe inter-symbol
and inter-carrier interference in conventional orthogonal frequency division
multiplexing (OFDM) systems \cite{shen2025,huang2026}.

Orthogonal time frequency space (OTFS) modulation exploits the quasi-static
properties of channels in the delay--Doppler domain to mitigate these effects
\cite{shen2025,hadani2017}. In \cite{shen2025}, multi-frame OTFS transmission
handles large differential delays and Doppler shifts at the satellite receiver,
allowing devices to operate without GNSS assistance or precompensation of these
offsets. Its effective channel has three indices at each antenna,
corresponding to Doppler, path delay, and received-symbol delay position
\cite[Sec.~II-B]{shen2025}. Affine frequency division multiplexing (AFDM)
provides an alternative based on one-dimensional chirp modulation. Its
modulator consists of an inverse DFT and two diagonal chirp multiplications
\cite[Secs.~II-B and III-A]{bemani2022}. With properly designed chirp
parameters, AFDM can achieve full diversity over doubly dispersive channels
\cite{bemani2022}. For the stationary-device channel considered here,
AFDM also permits joint processing of consecutive frames through a single
effective channel matrix per antenna and a device-specific phase rotation.
This compact representation motivates learning the effective-channel prior
directly for GFRA.

To realize the full potential of AFDM-GFRA, accurate joint activity detection and
channel estimation (JADCE) is a crucial prerequisite \cite{ding2026}. Existing
methods exploit sporadic device activity to formulate JADCE as a compressed sensing
(CS) problem and incorporate structured priors to capture channel sparsity
\cite{shen2025,ding2026,ke2020}. The scheme in \cite{ding2026} further uses a graph neural
network to adaptively learn sparsity patterns, while retaining a predefined
delay--Doppler grid for the sparse channel representation. In practical
propagation environments, significant power leakage caused by fractional Doppler
shifts and fractional time delays can weaken the sparsity of the effective channel
matrix \cite{huang2026}. This motivates learning effective-channel
priors from data to capture channel structures beyond the assumed sparse
representation \cite{cai2026,huang2026}.

Score-based generative models learn channel priors from samples by estimating the
score function of the channel distribution \cite{song2019,arvinte2023}. In
\cite{huang2026}, score-based learning is performed directly on the AFDM effective
channel to address fractional delay--Doppler off-grid leakage in channel estimation.
For massive random access, \cite{ying2026} proposes a two-stage algorithm that first
identifies active devices through a Transformer-based detector and then uses
generative diffusion models for joint channel estimation and data detection.
Both approaches rely on iterative posterior sampling, which requires
repeated score function evaluations and incurs substantial computational cost
\cite{huang2026,ying2026}.

The score-based turbo message passing (STMP) algorithm in \cite{cai2026}
incorporates generative channel priors for JADCE without iterative posterior
sampling. Through Tweedie's formulas, separate first- and second-order score networks provide
posterior means and variances for single-step minimum mean-squared error (MMSE)
denoising under equivalent additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) observations.
However, this AWGN model is justified in the large-system
limit with right-rotationally invariant random sensing matrices \cite{cai2026,rangan2019}.
In the finite-dimensional, structured multi-frame AFDM system considered here,
departures from these conditions may cause a mismatch between denoiser-input
errors and the white Gaussian noise used for training. A similar
limitation has been highlighted for structured compression matrices. This
mismatch can degrade channel denoising accuracy and, consequently, JADCE
performance. Moreover, \cite{cai2026} computes activity probabilities using
Gaussian extrinsic messages obtained after projecting the channel posterior onto
a Gaussian distribution. In general, matching posterior means and variances does
not preserve the marginal likelihood associated with a non-Gaussian channel
prior. Consequently, the resulting activity probabilities can be inaccurate,
affecting the channel estimates exchanged with the linear estimation module.

Against this background, we investigate GNSS-independent AFDM-GFRA for
LEO satellite IoT systems. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\arabic*)]
\item We propose a multi-frame AFDM transmission scheme that accommodates large
differential delays and Doppler shifts at the satellite receiver. Under the
common per-device Doppler model, a fixed effective channel matrix per antenna
is shared across frames, with inter-frame phase rotations incorporated into
the pilots. We compare this representation with the multi-frame OTFS model
at matched bandwidth and transmission duration. The resulting formulation
collects additional pilot observations without enlarging the channel tensor
used by the learned prior.

\item We learn a score-based generative prior directly from multiantenna AFDM
effective-channel samples with fractional delays and Doppler shifts, without
imposing sparse or grid-aligned channel assumptions.
To address the mismatch between denoiser-input errors and the white Gaussian
noise used for training, we train the denoiser using colored Gaussian noise
with different covariance matrices.

\item We develop a message-passing JADCE receiver for the multi-frame AFDM system.
The receiver combines multi-frame linear estimation (MFLE), which suppresses
inter-user interference, with generative-prior-aided joint denoising (GPJD),
which uses the learned effective-channel prior for MMSE denoising.
To reduce errors associated with a Gaussian approximation of the channel
posterior, GPJD employs a learned density-ratio estimator to obtain
posterior probabilities of activity. The two modules iteratively exchange
Gaussian extrinsic messages to perform JADCE.
Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed receiver improves activity
detection and channel estimation performance compared with the white-noise-trained
GP-MP reference across the evaluated signal-to-noise ratios and pilot-frame counts.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:system}
presents the system model and the multi-frame AFDM input--output relationship.
Sections~\ref{sec:algorithm}--\ref{sec:overall} describe the turbo message-passing
framework, the learning of channel and activity denoisers, and the overall algorithm with its computational
complexity analysis, respectively. Section~\ref{sec:simulations} presents the
simulation results. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes this paper.

\section{System Model}
\label{sec:system}

We consider a LEO satellite-enabled grant-free random access system
as shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:system-multiframe}, where AFDM is adopted
to mitigate the doubly dispersive effect inherent
in terrestrial-satellite links (TSLs) \cite{shen2025,huang2026}.
The system comprises $K$ single-antenna terrestrial devices that
communicate with a LEO satellite equipped with a uniform planar array
(UPA) consisting of $M=M_yM_z$ antennas.
During each transmission block, active devices share the same resources
for pilot transmission to the satellite.
These terrestrial devices operate without
GNSS capabilities and do not pre-compensate for delay and Doppler shifts
\cite{shen2025}.
\subsection{Terrestrial-Satellite Link Model}

The TSLs experience fast variations due to the high mobility of the
LEO satellite. Hence, this time variation and multipath propagation
require a doubly dispersive channel model \cite{shen2025}.
We assume that the terrestrial devices are stationary and
all paths from the $k$th device have a common Doppler shift $\nu_k$
\cite{huang2026}.
Within a transmission block, the path gains, delays, Doppler shifts,
and angles of arrival remain approximately constant.
We set $t_{\rm c}=0$ at the beginning of the transmission block.
After delay compensation for $\tau_c$ at the satellite receiver, the
channel impulse response from the $k$th device to the satellite at
time instant $t_{\rm c}$ can be represented as

\begin{equation}
 \mathbf h_k(t_{\rm c},\tau)
 =\mathbf a_k\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_k}g_{k\ell}
 e^{\mathrm j2\pi\nu_k t_{\rm c}}\delta(\tau-\tau_{k\ell}),
 \label{eq:physical-channel}
\end{equation}
where $k=1,\ldots,K$, $L_k$ is the number of physical paths,
$g_{k\ell}$ is the path gain of the $\ell$th path, and
$\delta(\cdot)$ is the Dirac delta function, and $\mathrm j^2=-1$.
Here $\tau_{k\ell}=\widetilde\tau_{k\ell}-\tau_c$ represents the
differential delay for the $\ell$th path from the $k$th device to the
satellite, where $\widetilde\tau_{k\ell}$ and $\tau_c$ are denoted as
propagation delay and common delay, respectively.
The common delay corresponds to the
propagation time between the satellite and the closest point on Earth
within the beam coverage \cite{shen2025}.

\subsection{Transmission Scheme}
\label{sec:transmission-scheme}

In the proposed scheme, each active device transmits pilot symbols over
$Q$ consecutive AFDM frames within one transmission block.
AFDM modulation and demodulation are performed independently for each
frame, and the received signals are collected for JADCE.
A total of $N$ chirp subcarriers are shared among the devices for
pilot transmission \cite{cai2026,huang2026}.
Let $P_{qkn}\in\mathbb C$ be the pilot symbol transmitted by
the $k$-th device during the $q$-th AFDM frame on the $n$-th
chirp subcarrier. We construct a pilot vector as
$\mathbf p_{qk}=[P_{qk0},\ldots,P_{qk,N-1}]^{\mathsf T}
\in\mathbb C^N$, $k=1,\ldots,K$, $q=0,\ldots,Q-1$, where
$(\cdot)^{\mathsf T}$ denotes transpose.
The pilot symbols are known at the satellite receiver.
Let $\mathbf P\in\mathbb C^{Q\times KN}$ denote the pilot matrix,
with entries
$[\mathbf P]_{q,(k-1)N+n}=P_{qkn}$.

We impose the condition that
$\mathbf P\mathbf P^{\mathsf H}=KE_p\I_Q$, where
$\|\mathbf p_{qk}\|^2=E_p$ for all $k$ and $q$
\cite{cai2026}.
Here $\I_Q$ is the $Q\times Q$ identity matrix.
The design of $\mathbf P$ is deferred to
Section~\ref{sec:simulation-settings}.

In \eqref{eq:channel}, the effective channel at each antenna is
represented by an $N\times N$ matrix. The multi-frame OTFS scheme in
\cite[eq.~(9)]{shen2025} uses an $L\times N\times N$ tensor for $N$
subcarriers and $L$ OFDM symbols per frame. The dense AFDM channel representation
contains $MN^2$ channel entries per device, compared with
$MLN^2$ in that OTFS representation. With the same subcarrier spacing
and prefix length, $L$ AFDM frames span the duration of one OTFS
frame, with the same number of useful samples and the same useful-symbol
energy when the OTFS frame uses $LE_p$.
\subsection{Problem Formulation}

Each device determines whether to access the channel in an independent
and identically distributed (i.i.d.) manner.
We use a binary activity variable $\alpha_k$, defined as
\cite{cai2026}
\[
 \alpha_k=\begin{cases}
 1,&\text{if the $k$th device is active},\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Let $\rho$ represent the probability of a device being active, i.e.,
$\Pr(\alpha_k=1)=\rho$, where $\rho\ll1$.
As a result, only a small subset of the devices is active in any given
transmission block. The activity states are
assumed to remain constant during one block transmission.
Let $X_k=\alpha_kH_k$.

We express the received signal $\mathbf Y$ over the $Q$ AFDM frames
in a more compact form as
\begin{equation}
 \mathbf Y=\mathbf A\mathbf X+\mathbf W,
 \label{eq:mmv}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf Y,\mathbf W\in\mathbb C^{Q\times MN}$,
$\mathbf A\in\mathbb C^{Q\times KN}$, and
$\mathbf X\in\mathbb C^{KN\times MN}$.
The matrices $\mathbf Y$, $\mathbf W$, $\mathbf A$, and $\mathbf X$
have the following entries:
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 [\mathbf Y]_{q,mN+r}&=Y_{qmr},\\
 [\mathbf W]_{q,mN+r}&=W_{qmr},\\
 [\mathbf A]_{q,(k-1)N+n}&=A_{qkn},\\
 [\mathbf X]_{(k-1)N+n,mN+r}&=X_{kmrn}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:mmv-indexing}
\end{equation}
Since the $Q$ frames share the same $\mathbf X$, additional pilot
frames provide more observations without increasing the number of
channel coefficients to be estimated.
Due to the sporadic access of the devices, $\mathbf X$ exhibits a
block-sparsity structure.
Specifically, if the $k$th device is inactive, we have
$X_k=\alpha_kH_k=\mathbf0$ \cite{cai2026}.
For $Q<KN$, the inverse problem in \eqref{eq:mmv} is underdetermined.

In this paper, we aim to simultaneously detect the active devices and
estimate the corresponding channels based on the observation $\mathbf Y$
under a Bayesian inference framework \cite{cai2026}.
Power leakage arises from fractional delays and Doppler shifts,
which can weaken the sparsity of $H_k$ \cite{huang2026}.
We therefore estimate the full $H_k$ without imposing channel sparsity.
We use the distribution of the training channels as the channel prior
$q_{\rm tr}(H_k)$, without factorizing this prior element-wise.
We assume that $H_k$ and $\alpha_k$ are independent for different
values of $k$, and that $H_k$ is independent of $\alpha_k$.
With $\widehat{\mathbf A}$ and $\widehat\sigma^2$ fixed as in

theorem and the conditional independence relationships among the

\section{Learning Channel and Activity Denoisers}
\label{sec:learning}

We learn a channel denoiser using the score-function representation of
\eqref{eq:conditional-channel-integrals} \cite[Sec.~IV-A]{cai2026}, and
learn the density ratio required for \eqref{eq:local-activity}.

\subsection{Bridging Score Function and MMSE Denoising}
\label{sec:score-denoising}

Consider the channel observation under the active hypothesis in
\eqref{eq:pseudo-awgn}.
For a complex-valued channel sample $H\sim q_{\rm tr}$, we stack the
real and imaginary parts of $\vect(H)$ in $\mathbf h_{\mathbb
R}\in\mathbb R^{2D}$.
To allow for correlated errors, we consider an independent proper
complex Gaussian perturbation with covariance $\mathbf C\succ0$, giving the real
observation
\begin{equation}
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathbf u=\mathbf h_{\mathbb R}+\bm\Sigma^{1/2}\bm\epsilon,
 \qquad \bm\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf0,\I_{2D}),\\
 \bm\Sigma=\frac12
 \begin{bmatrix}\Re \mathbf C&-\Im \mathbf C\\\Im \mathbf C&\Re \mathbf C\end{bmatrix}.
 \end{gathered}
 \label{eq:colored-query}
\end{equation}

The gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf u}\log q_{\bm\Sigma}^{\mathbb R}$ is the
first-order score function \cite{hyvarinen2005}.
For $\mathbf C=v\I_D$, \eqref{eq:tweedie-mean} gives the real representation of
the conditional mean in \eqref{eq:conditional-channel-integrals}.

\subsection{First-Order Score Matching}
\label{sec:channel-learning}

The expectation is taken over the clean channels, perturbation
covariances, and Gaussian noise.
For each fixed $\mathbf C$, the conditional mean $\mathbf m_{\mathbb R}(\mathbf
u,\mathbf C)$ minimizes this loss over unrestricted mean functions.

During message passing, the denoiser receives observations with
different noise variances.
We therefore train over a range of perturbation variances, as in
\cite[Sec.~IV-B]{cai2026}.
The input errors in the finite-dimensional multi-frame model can also be
correlated.
To account for this correlation, we corrupt clean channel samples with
colored Gaussian noise of covariance $\mathbf C=v(\mathbf R_{\rm a}\otimes\I_N\otimes
\mathbf R_{\rm c})$ in antenna--output--input order and condition the network on
$\mathbf C$ \cite[Sec.~III-B]{shastri2022}.
The covariance factors and the sampling law for $v$ are specified in
Section~\ref{sec:training-settings}.

Reshaping the real and imaginary outputs of $f_\theta$ defines the

For the scalar-variance message in \eqref{eq:pseudo-awgn}, we evaluate

\section{GP-MP-CCD Algorithm}
\label{sec:overall}

\subsection{Overall Algorithm}
\label{sec:schedule}

GP-MP-CCD combines the multi-frame linear estimation (MFLE) in
Section~\ref{sec:linear-estimation} with generative-prior-aided joint
denoising (GPJD) using the estimators in Section~\ref{sec:learning}.
Fig.~\ref{fig:learned-receiver} shows their message exchange.

For a Gaussian input $(R_k,v)$, the denoiser gives
$F_k=F_\theta(R_k,v\I_D)$, and the classifier gives $p_k$ in
\eqref{eq:activity-probability}. With
$\widehat\tau_k=\widehat\tau_\theta(R_k,v\I_D)$ from
\eqref{eq:derivative-trace}, we use the common conditional variance
\begin{equation}
 \tau_{\rm raw}=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\widehat\tau_k,\qquad
 \tau^{\rm post}=\max\{\tau_{\rm raw},\tau_{\min}\}.
 \label{eq:pooled-variance}
\end{equation}
Here $\tau_{\min}>0$ is a numerical floor.

Algorithm~1 combines these estimates with $p_k$ and returns Gaussian
extrinsic messages to MFLE. Estimated phases are refined as in
Appendix~\ref{app:phase-refinement}. After normalization,
we initialize $\mathbf X^{{\rm pri},(0)}=\mathbf0$,
$\gamma^{(0)}=\rho\widehat P_H$, $E_k=0$, $c_k=1$, and
$\kappa^{(1)}=1$, where $\widehat P_H$ is the training average
of $\norm{H}_F^2/D$.

Appendix~\ref{app:frontend} estimates the phases used to form
$\widehat{\mathbf A}$, which is fixed between phase refinements.
For noise estimation, let
$\mathbf y_{qr}=(Y_{q0r},\ldots,Y_{q,M-1,r})^{\mathsf T}$ and
$N_{\rm s}=QN>M\geq2$. The spatial sample covariance and noise estimate are
\begin{equation}
 \widehat{\mathbf R}_y=\frac1{N_{\rm s}}\sum_{q,r}
 \mathbf y_{qr}\mathbf y_{qr}^{\mathsf H},\qquad
 \widehat\sigma^2=\frac{\sum_{i=\widehat r_{\rm s}+1}^{M}\lambda_i}
 {M-\widehat r_{\rm s}}.
 \label{eq:noise-estimation}
\end{equation}
Here $\lambda_1\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_M$ are the covariance eigenvalues,
and $\widehat r_{\rm s}$ is selected by the Wax--Kailath minimum
description length (MDL) criterion \cite{wax1985,nadakuditi2008}.
Under a lower-rank spatial signal plus white noise, this estimate remains
fixed during MP.

The first input and feedback messages are used without damping.
Stopping checks and numerical settings are given in
Section~\ref{sec:simulation-settings}.

\subsection{Computational Complexity Analysis}
\label{sec:complexity}

With precomputed chirp factors, $L$ AFDM frames require at most
$LC_{\rm FFT}(N)+2LN$ complex multiplications
\cite[eq.~(16)]{bemani2022}, where $C_{\rm FFT}(n)$ is the cost of an
$n$-point FFT or inverse FFT. For the same $LN$ useful symbols,
rectangular-pulse OTFS with an identity transmit window requires
$NC_{\rm FFT}(L)$ after transform cancellation
\cite{zou2021otfs}.
Their ordering depends on $N$, $L$, and the FFT implementation.
The following costs concern JADCE after waveform demodulation.

Here $\mathbf R_{\rm L}=\mathbf X^{\rm pri} +(\mathbf X_{\rm L}-\mathbf
X^{\rm pri})/f_{\rm L}$.
SVD and noise estimation cost $O(KNQ^2)$ and $O(QNM^2+M^3)$
per block, respectively. Let $C_{\rm phase}$ denote the phase-search,
refinement, and gain-estimation cost in Appendix~\ref{app:frontend}.
Per iteration, MFLE transformations cost $O(QKMN^2)$, spatial covariance
operations cost $O(KM^2N^2)$, and matrix factorizations cost $O(M^3)$.
Let $C_\theta,C_\phi$ denote the per-device denoiser and classifier costs.
The $1+2L_z$ denoiser evaluations and one classifier evaluation within the
training interval give the per-iteration complexity
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 C_{\rm iter}=O\bigl(&QKMN^2+KM^2N^2+M^3\\
 &+K[(1+2L_z)C_\theta+C_\phi]\bigr).
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:iteration-complexity}
\end{equation}

For $I$ iterations, the total online complexity is
$O(C_{\rm phase}+QNM^2+M^3+KNQ^2+I C_{\rm iter})$.

Here $C_{\rm phase}=0$ for supplied phases; each phase refinement also
requires a new $O(KNQ^2)$ SVD. With shared network parameters, working storage
is $O(QKN+KMN^2+KM^2)$ for pilot/SVD factors, channel messages, and spatial
covariances, excluding parameters and network activations.

\subsubsection{Network Architectures}
\label{sec:network-settings}

The denoiser uses the RefineNet \cite{lin2017} variant in
\cite[Appendix~A]{song2019}, with $2M$ real/imaginary input maps over
$N\times N$ DAFT coordinates. Its four stages have $(128,256,256,256)$
channels and two residual blocks each, with two $3\times3$ convolutions,
conditional instance normalization, and exponential linear unit (ELU)
activations per block. Stage~2 halves the resolution; stages~3--4 retain it
with dilations $2$ and $4$. Four refinement blocks with
$(256,256,128,128)$ channels combine the stage outputs and restore the
resolution; input/output projections use $3\times3$ convolutions.
For conditioning, $\log(v)/5$ and flattened real/imaginary entries of
$\mathbf R_{\rm a}-\I_M$ and $\mathbf R_{\rm c}-\I_N$ pass through two
$64$-unit fully connected layers with sigmoid-weighted linear unit (SiLU)
activations, followed by linear projections to the normalization layers.
We extend the scalar preconditioning in \cite[Sec.~5]{karras2022} to
\begin{equation}
 \begin{aligned}
 f_\theta(\mathbf u,\mathbf C)
 &=\mathbf K_{\bm\Sigma}\mathbf u
   +\mathbf O_{\bm\Sigma}g_\theta
       (\mathbf B_{\bm\Sigma}\mathbf u,\mathbf C),\\
 \mathbf B_{\bm\Sigma}
 &=(\sigma_{\rm d}^2\I_{2D}+\bm\Sigma)^{-1/2},\\
 \mathbf K_{\bm\Sigma}
 &=\sigma_{\rm d}^2(\sigma_{\rm d}^2\I_{2D}+\bm\Sigma)^{-1},\\
 \mathbf O_{\bm\Sigma}
 &=\sigma_{\rm d}\bigl[
 \bm\Sigma(\sigma_{\rm d}^2\I_{2D}+\bm\Sigma)^{-1}\bigr]^{1/2}.
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:mean-preconditioning}
\end{equation}

Here $\sigma_{\rm d}^2=1/2$ is the nominal normalized variance per
real coordinate, and $g_\theta$ is the backbone.

The classifier takes $4M$ real/imaginary maps of $R$ and
$F_\theta(R,v\I_D)$, scaled by $\sqrt{2/(1+v)}$, plus five scalars:
$\log(v)/5$, logarithmic transforms of input/output/residual energies
normalized by $Dv$, and a sign-preserving logarithmic transform of the
real inner product normalized by $Dv$.
Three stages contain two $3\times3$ convolutions each, with
$(64,128,128)$ channels, SiLU, and padding $1$. The first convolution
of stages~2--3 has stride $2$; all others have stride $1$.
A $64$-unit fully connected SiLU layer embeds $\log(v)/5$; its linear
projections are added to each stage output. Flattened features and the
five scalars pass through fully connected layers of widths $(128,1)$,
with SiLU between them, yielding one logit per device.

\subsubsection{Stopping Criteria}
\label{sec:stopping-criteria}

After $I_{\min}$ iterations, stopping requires stable channel estimates,
input variance, and activity probabilities, agreement between the input and target
variances, and accepted, stable Gaussian site updates for five
consecutive iterations, together with unchanged activity decisions
for ten iterations. Otherwise, the last iterate is returned
at $I_{\max}$.

\subsection{Channel Denoising Performance}
\label{sec:denoising-performance}

Following \cite[Sec.~VI-B]{cai2026}, denoising uses $R=H+W$,
$\vect(W)\sim\CN(\mathbf0,v\I)$, with known $v$ and nominal SNR
$-10\log_{10}v$. At each of six SNRs from $-20$ to $30$~dB, both
neural estimators share $2{,}000$ samples from $500$ scenes and the
same white-noise realizations.

References are least squares (LS), returning $R$; the Gaussian-prior
estimate $\widehat P_H R/(\widehat P_H+v)$, using the training-channel
power defined in Section~\ref{sec:schedule}; and genie-aided conditional MMSE.
Given true path geometry, powers, and line-of-sight gain, the genie
reports the analytic conditional MSE of the remaining Gaussian gains.
The four sparse-recovery methods use an identity observation operator
and known AWGN variance, retaining their receiver settings and GNN
weights; GAMP-SBL retains its internal noise update.

Figure~\ref{fig:cstmp-denoising} shows that both learned denoisers
improve with SNR, whereas the sparse-recovery curves approach an error
floor. Colored-noise training further improves denoising at low SNR.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

% Included in both manuscript versions on 2026-11-03 at the author's request.
In this paper, we investigated GNSS-independent GFRA for LEO satellite
IoT. We proposed a multi-frame AFDM transmission scheme to accommodate
large differential delays and Doppler shifts, using a shared
effective-channel representation to collect additional pilot observations
without increasing the channel dimension. Based on this model, we learned
a score-based generative prior from multiantenna AFDM effective channels
without imposing sparse or grid-aligned channel assumptions, with colored
Gaussian noise used to account for correlations in denoiser-input errors.
We then developed a JADCE receiver that combines multi-frame linear
estimation with generative-prior-aided joint denoising, where learned
density ratios provide posterior activity probabilities. Simulation
results demonstrated improved channel estimation and activity detection
over the white-noise-trained baseline, reduced pilot requirements at the
evaluated accuracy target, and channel-estimation gains across the tested
NTN-TDL profiles without retraining. These results support the use of
learned effective-channel priors for multi-frame AFDM random access in
LEO satellite systems.

\subsection{Phase Refinement During Message Passing}
\label{app:phase-refinement}

Following \cite[Sec.~III-C]{shen2025}, refinement fixes the Gaussian
feedback message and computes the conditional channel mean and covariance under
the observation model. It minimizes the expected squared observation
residual, retaining cross-device conditional covariances and the
constraint $e^{\mathrm jq\beta_k}$. Coordinate updates optimize $\beta_k$ and a constant phase for each
device, absorbing the constant phase into the feedback means. Each refinement uses two to ten sweeps
with relative objective-change tolerance $10^{-7}$.

After a phase update, we rebuild $\widehat{\mathbf A}$ and its SVD,
clear the input-damping history, set $\kappa=1$, and reset the stopping
windows. The channel sites and rotated feedback are retained.

\section{Receiver Configurations and Evaluation Protocol}
\label{app:evaluation-protocol}

\subsection{Learned Receiver Configurations}
\label{app:receiver-configurations}

GP-MP follows the STMP framework \cite{cai2026} adapted to the AFDM
model, with learned activity probabilities replacing the analytical activity
update. It uses a white-noise-trained first-order score network, a
learned second-order network, and a learned density-ratio classifier.
GP-MP-CCD uses the denoiser conditioned on the noise covariance and preconditioning
in Section~\ref{sec:network-settings}, its derivative-based variance
estimate, the corresponding activity classifier, and the input
variance update in \eqref{eq:query-variance-update}.
The two configurations use the same clean training channels and number of
denoiser training epochs.
Thus the complete-receiver comparison evaluates the two adopted
configurations; it does not isolate the training covariance as their
only difference. The activity-probability comparison instead changes
only the probability calculation specified in
Section~\ref{sec:activity-evidence}.
\subsection{Paired Scenes and Parameter Selection}

The comparisons in Section~\ref{sec:simulations} use saved, paired physical
scenes. The SNR figure uses scenes $0$--$499$ at each point for all
receivers. The known-phase curves are recomputed from saved predictions
of the original $1{,}000$-scene experiment to match the completed
estimated-phase batch; the original full-batch results are preserved.
The pilot comparison uses the first $500$ of the planned $1{,}000$
scenes. The device-count, activity-probability, and cross-profile
comparisons also use scenes $0$--$499$ at each condition.
Development and baseline-threshold selection
overlap the evaluation scenes; the adopted baseline activity decision rules are
reused without refitting. The reported SNR range was narrowed after
interim inspection; the earlier $8$ and $10$~dB results remain archived.
All finite outputs enter the reported metrics, including those that
reach the iteration limit.

\subsection{Activity Probability Comparison}
\label{app:activity-evidence-protocol}

The experiment using the Gaussian approximation for activity detection was stopped after
inspection of its adverse results, with $2{,}128$ outputs saved. The
common subset in Table~\ref{tab:activity-evidence} contains every one
of the $354$ physical scenes with completed outputs at all six SNRs,
giving $2{,}124$ condition evaluations per method. The same subset is
used for the complete receiver. AER pools all device decisions across
these conditions, including outputs that reach the iteration limit.
The four outputs from the partially completed next scene remain
archived. This is a retrospective comparison over the common completed
scenes, not the originally planned $1{,}000$-scene sweep; the six SNRs
do not constitute independent physical scenes.

Within this paired subset, $724$ of the $2{,}124$ runs using the Gaussian approximation
reach the iteration limit. The learned density ratio and Gaussian approximation
produce $(111,3)$ and $(187,31{,}207)$ missed detections and false
alarms, respectively, over $84{,}960$ device decisions. These counts
give the pooled AER values in Table~\ref{tab:activity-evidence}; the
large error increase is dominated by false alarms. They describe the
tested receiver substitution and do not by themselves identify the
cause of nonconvergence.

\subsection{Estimated-Phase Evaluation}
\label{app:estimated-phase-protocol}

The estimated-phase curve uses the completed batch of $500$ scenes
at each of six SNRs. The receiver receives the observations, original
pilots, and activity prior; true phases, activity, channels, and noise
variance are unavailable to inference. The phase configuration was
selected using $13$ scenes that are included in the displayed batch.
Consequently, this comparison is retrospective rather than an
independent test of the phase-update settings. The other receivers in
Fig.~\ref{fig:cstmp-snr} use known phases.

Phase refinement is checked every $20$ iterations, starting at
iteration $20$. A check is eligible when the conditional estimates
have met the relative-change and activity-change tolerances for five
iterations, the decisions have remained stable for ten iterations,
and the current channel mean and covariance estimates are valid. After at least one phase
update, stopping compares the channel estimate and received-signal
prediction at successive eligible checks. It requires relative
changes below $0.05$, ten iterations with stable decisions and valid mean and covariance estimates,
at least $80$ total iterations, and at least ten iterations since the
last phase update. The maximum is $600$ iterations. One of the
$3{,}000$ outputs reaches this limit and is retained. These settings
differ from the known-phase stopping rule; the SNR figure compares
estimation and detection accuracy, not equal computational budgets.
\subsection{Device-Count-Specific Damping}

GP-MP uses damping factor $0.2$ at $K=20,40$ and $0.1$ at
$K=60,80,100$. The latter was selected after inspecting the original
$500$-scene results at weight $0.2$ and a $12$-input diagnostic at weight
$0.1$. All $12$ diagnostic inputs are included in the reported panels.
With the original weight, $498$, $479$, and $500$ scenes reached the
iteration limit at $K=60,80,100$, respectively; those outputs remain
archived. Under the adopted settings, all $500$ scenes converge at
$K=20,40,60$, while $3$ and $14$ reach the limit at $K=80$ and $100$.
These $17$ outputs are retained in the NMSE.

For GP-MP-CCD, the weight was reduced from $0.4$ to $0.2$ for all
$K=100$ scenes after preliminary inspection. At $K=80$, only scene~372
was rerun with weight $0.2$ after its original run reached the iteration
limit; this selected replacement is used in the reported panel. Other
$K=80$ scenes retain weight $0.4$. Both receivers retain the same
$60$--$600$ iteration limits and stopping criteria. These settings
constitute retrospective parameter development, rather than independent
validation of a fixed damping rule across all candidate device counts.

\subsection{Additional Implementation Settings}
\label{app:implementation-settings}

The normalization constant is $s=0.2647966453$.
The activity-change, site-parameter, and activity-history tolerances
are $10^{-3}$, $0.1$, and $10^{-3}$, respectively, with
$\zeta_{\rm hist}=0.2$, $L_s=5$, and $L_d=10$.

The estimate check monitors relative changes in $\widehat X$ and $v$,
the maximum activity change $\max_k|p_k^{(i)}-p_k^{(i-1)}|$, and
$d_{\rm var}^{(i)}=|v_{\rm tar}^{(i)}-v^{(i)}|/
\max\{v_{\rm tar}^{(i)},v^{(i)}\}$.
The site check requires accepted updates with stable precision
$c_k^{-1}$ and natural parameter $E_k/c_k$, together with a small
activity-history residual $\max_k|p_k^{(i)}-w_k^{(i-1)}|$.
After this comparison, update
$w_k^{(i)}=(1-\zeta_{\rm hist})w_k^{(i-1)}+\zeta_{\rm hist} p_k^{(i)}$, starting from
$w_k^{(0)}=\rho$.
After $I_{\min}$ iterations, both checks must hold for $L_s$
consecutive iterations and hard activity decisions must remain unchanged
for $L_d$ iterations; otherwise, return the last iterate at $I_{\max}$.
